Let $n\ge 1$, let $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The corresponding **permutation matrix** $P_\sigma$ is the
matrix whose $i$-th row is the $\sigma(i)$-th row of $I_n$. Thus left
multiplication by $P_\sigma$ permutes the rows of a matrix.

In **Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting**, ties are resolved by a fixed
deterministic rule. At stage $k$ one inspects the
entries in column $k$ from rows $k$ through $n-1$, swaps a row with maximal
entry modulus into row $k$, and then eliminates the entries below that pivot.

If $PA=LU$ is the resulting factorisation, its **pivot-growth factor** is

$$\rho(A):=\frac{\max_{i,j}|u_{ij}|}{\max_{i,j}|a_{ij}|},$$

provided $A\ne 0$; when $A=0$ one declares $\rho(A)=1$. The absolute value or
modulus is the one from [[def-abs-value]] on real entries and its standard
complex analogue on complex entries.

Start from $S^{(0)}=PAP^T$. Maintain a row permutation $Q$, a unit lower-triangular factor $L$, and the current active matrix. Every real scalar operation uses [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]; if an exact intermediate is nonzero and subnormal, overflows, or the operation reports range failure, return **range-failure** at its stage. The pivot tests and tie-breaking comparisons are exact guards on the current stored values. For $k=0,\ldots,n-1$, ties for a maximum are resolved by choosing the smallest current row index.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\in\mathbb N$ (including $0$), and let $A\in M_{n\times n}(F)$ satisfy
$A_{ij}=A_{ji}$ for every $i,j<n$ (that is, $A$ is symmetric). Its
**structural graph** is
the simple undirected graph $G_0=(V,E_0)$ with vertex set
$V=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and edge set

$$E_0:=\bigl\{\{i,j\}:0\le i<j<n,\ A_{ij}\ne0\bigr\}.$$

An **elimination ordering** is a listing $v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}$ in which every
vertex of $V$ occurs exactly once. Define the current vertex set by
$V_k=\{v_\ell:k\le\ell<n\}$, starting with the structural graph $G_0$. At
step $k$, the **later neighbors** of $v_k$ are

$$N_k(v_k):=\{u\in V_k\setminus\{v_k\}:\{u,v_k\}\in E_k\}.$$

The filled graph $G_{k+1}=(V_{k+1},E_{k+1})$ is obtained by deleting $v_k$ and
its incident edges, retaining all edges between remaining vertices, and adding
every edge between two distinct vertices of $N_k(v_k)$. An edge added at step
$k$ that was not already in $E_k$ is a **fill edge**. Repeating this rule
defines the symbolic elimination pattern for the ordering; it is defined from
the initial graph and ordering alone, without numerical pivot values.

If $N_k(v_k)$ is nonempty, the **parent** of $v_k$ is the later neighbor
$v_\ell$ with least position $\ell>k$ in the ordering. If $N_k(v_k)$ is
empty, $v_k$ is a root. Each non-root has a unique parent, and positions strictly increase along parent edges, so there is no directed cycle. If the underlying undirected graph had a cycle, its least-position vertex would be a child of both adjacent later vertices, contradicting uniqueness. Thus the parent relation is an elimination forest.

derivations.claim: At $k=0$, a walk with no internal vertices consists of one edge, so the claimed equivalence is exactly the definition of $G_0$.

Suppose the equivalence holds at stage $k$. A retained edge in $G_{k+1}$ already has a witnessing walk whose internal vertices are among $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$. An edge newly added at step $k$ joins two vertices $x,y$ that are each adjacent to $v_k$ in $G_k$. The induction hypothesis gives walks from $x$ to $v_k$ and from $v_k$ to $y$ with internal vertices among $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$; concatenating them gives the required walk with the additional internal vertex $v_k$. This proves the forward implication at stage $k+1$.

Conversely, let a witnessing walk from $x$ to $y$ have internal vertices among $v_0,\ldots,v_k$. If it has no internal occurrence of $v_k$, the induction hypothesis gives an edge in $G_k$, which is retained. Otherwise take the first and last internal occurrences of $v_k$. The initial subwalk from $x$ to the first occurrence and the terminal subwalk from the last occurrence to $y$ have all internal vertices among $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$. By induction, $x$ and $y$ are both later neighbors of $v_k$ in $G_k$. Since $x\ne y$, the update inserts $\{x,y\}$ in $G_{k+1}$.
The base case and steps 1.2 and 2.1 prove both implications for every stage by induction on $k$.

derivations.claim: The initial active matrix is $PAP^T$, whose entrywise maximum is $M$ because $P$ only permutes rows and columns; hence $\rho\ge1$. Let $c=S^{(k)}_{ik}$ and $p=S^{(k)}_{kk}$ at a successful pivot. If the diagonal is accepted, [F1] gives $|c/p|\le\theta^{-1}$. If a maximum-modulus entry is selected, $|c/p|\le1\le\theta^{-1}$. The rounded division therefore gives $|\widehat l_{ik}|\le(1+u)/\theta\le2/\theta$. Also every pivot-row entry and every active entry has modulus at most $\rho M$.

For a trailing update, write $p_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kj})$ and $S^{(k+1)}_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(S^{(k)}_{ij}-p_{ij})$. Define $e_{ijk}=S^{(k+1)}_{ij}-(S^{(k)}_{ij}-\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kj})$. By [F2]. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
$$
|p_{ij}-\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kj}|\le u|\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kj}|,
\quad
|S^{(k+1)}_{ij}-(S^{(k)}_{ij}-p_{ij})|\le u|S^{(k)}_{ij}-p_{ij}|.
$$
The triangle inequality and $|p_{ij}|\le(1+u)|\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kj}|$ yield
$$
|e_{ijk}|\le u|S^{(k)}_{ij}|+u(2+u)|\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kj}|
\le u\rho M\left(1+\frac{(2+u)(1+u)}{\theta}\right)
\le \frac{7u\rho M}{\theta},
$$
using $u<1$ and $\theta\le1$.
For a computed multiplier, $\widehat l_{ik}=\operatorname{fl}(c/p)$, so [F2] gives a division residual $e^{\rm div}_{ik}:=c-\widehat l_{ik}p$ with $|e^{\rm div}_{ik}|\le u|c|\le u\rho M$.

Track each active row together with its previously stored entries of $\widehat L$ and its accumulated update residuals. Before stage $k$, for every active row $i$ and active column $j\ge k$, maintain [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, induction, algebra]
$$
(Q_k P A P^T)_{ij}=\sum_{r<k}\widehat l_{ir}\widehat u_{rj}+S^{(k)}_{ij}-\sum_{r<k}e_{ijr},
$$
where $Q_k$ is the row permutation accumulated so far. At $k=0$ this is $S^{(0)}=PAP^T$. Swapping two active rows also swaps their earlier $L$ entries and residual histories, so it preserves the invariant. After the pivot, $\widehat u_{kj}=S^{(k)}_{kj}$; each lower-row update is $S^{(k+1)}_{ij}=S^{(k)}_{ij}-\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kj}+e_{ijk}$, so substitution gives the same invariant at stage $k+1$. For the pivot column, $S^{(k)}_{ik}=\widehat l_{ik}\widehat u_{kk}+e^{\rm div}_{ik}$ by definition of the division residual. Thus after all stages, for $i\le j$,
$$
(\widehat QPA P^T)_{ij}-(\widehat L\widehat U)_{ij}=-\sum_{k<i}e_{ijk},
$$
and for $i>j$,
$$
(\widehat QPA P^T)_{ij}-(\widehat L\widehat U)_{ij}
=e^{\rm div}_{ij}-\sum_{k<j}e_{ijk}.
$$
These identities define $\Delta A=\widehat L\widehat U-\widehat QPA P^T$. Each entry contains at most $n$ update residuals and at most one division residual.

By steps 1.2–2.1, every residual entry is bounded by [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]
$$
n\frac{7u\rho M}{\theta}+u\rho M
\le \frac{8nu}{\theta}\rho M,
$$
since $n\ge1$ and $\theta\le1$. Summing at most $n$ such bounds in any row gives $\|\Delta A\|_\infty\le8n^2u\rho M/\theta$.

The definition of $\Delta A$ in step 3.1 gives the displayed nearby-factorization identity, and step 4.1 gives both residual bounds. The only growth quantity in the estimate is the maximum active-entry magnitude of this executed run.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\in\mathbb N$ (including $0$), and let $A\in M_{n\times n}(F)$ satisfy
$A_{ij}=A_{ji}$ for every $i,j<n$ (that is, $A$ is symmetric). Its
**structural graph** is
the simple undirected graph $G_0=(V,E_0)$ with vertex set
$V=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and edge set

$$E_0:=\bigl\{\{i,j\}:0\le i<j<n,\ A_{ij}\ne0\bigr\}.$$

An **elimination ordering** is a listing $v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}$ in which every
vertex of $V$ occurs exactly once. Define the current vertex set by
$V_k=\{v_\ell:k\le\ell<n\}$, starting with the structural graph $G_0$. At
step $k$, the **later neighbors** of $v_k$ are

$$N_k(v_k):=\{u\in V_k\setminus\{v_k\}:\{u,v_k\}\in E_k\}.$$

The filled graph $G_{k+1}=(V_{k+1},E_{k+1})$ is obtained by deleting $v_k$ and
its incident edges, retaining all edges between remaining vertices, and adding
every edge between two distinct vertices of $N_k(v_k)$. An edge added at step
$k$ that was not already in $E_k$ is a **fill edge**. Repeating this rule
defines the symbolic elimination pattern for the ordering; it is defined from
the initial graph and ordering alone, without numerical pivot values.

If $N_k(v_k)$ is nonempty, the **parent** of $v_k$ is the later neighbor
$v_\ell$ with least position $\ell>k$ in the ordering. If $N_k(v_k)$ is
empty, $v_k$ is a root. Each non-root has a unique parent, and positions strictly increase along parent edges, so there is no directed cycle. If the underlying undirected graph had a cycle, its least-position vertex would be a child of both adjacent later vertices, contradicting uniqueness. Thus the parent relation is an elimination forest.

Input an integer $k\ge1$ and dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. The coordinate vertices are $\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d$. Identify them with the zero-based matrix indices $0,\ldots,k^d-1$ by the lexicographic bijection $q(i_1,\ldots,i_d)=\sum_{a=1}^d i_a k^{d-a}$. The grid graph has an edge between two coordinate vertices exactly when they differ by $1$ in one coordinate and agree in all others. Use the graph and ordering conventions of [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]] on these indices. Thus $d=2$ gives the five-point graph and $d=3$ the seven-point graph.

Order a rectangular coordinate subbox recursively as follows. For each coordinate whose side length is at least $2$, choose its lower median coordinate, namely the coordinate with $\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor$ positions below it in a side of length $m$. Let $S$ be the union of the coordinate hyperplanes at those selected medians. Delete $S$, obtaining at most $2^d$ nonempty rectangular child boxes. Recursively order the child boxes in lexicographic order of their lower corners, then append the vertices of $S$ in lexicographic order. If no coordinate has side length at least $2$, append the remaining vertex as a terminal separator. Apply this rule first to the whole grid. The resulting order is the **coordinate nested-dissection ordering**.

The recursion uses only the graph geometry. It makes no fill or complexity claim for arbitrary graphs.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and use the coordinate grid and recursive ordering of [[alg-nested-dissection-ordering-on-regular-grids]]. For a recursion box $B$, let $S_B$ be its median separator; for the terminal one-vertex box take $S_B=B$. Let $\partial^+B$ be the set of grid vertices outside $B$ adjacent to some vertex of $B$. If $v\in S_B$, then every later filled neighbor of $v$ lies in $S_B\cup\partial^+B$. If every side of $B$ has length at most $s$, then
$$
|\{v\}\cup N^+_\pi(v)|\le |S_B|+|\partial^+B|\le 3d\,s^{d-1}.
$$

Use the zero-based graph and ordering of [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]]. For distinct remaining vertices $x,y\in V_k$, the pair $\{x,y\}$ is an edge of $G_k$ if and only if the original graph $G_0$ contains a finite walk from $x$ to $y$ all of whose internal vertices belong to $\{v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}\}$. A walk may repeat vertices; its internal vertices are the entries other than its two endpoints.

Assume exact arithmetic, a Hermitian positive-definite $A$, and a successful ordered factorization using [[alg-multifrontal-cholesky-and-sparse-triangular-solves]]. The fronts and contribution arrays give the same Cholesky factor as scalar elimination in ordering $\pi$. With $d_r=\ell_r+1=|F_r|$, the arithmetic work for assembly and scalar front updates is
$$O\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^n d_r^2\right),$$
the symbolic factor allocation has exactly $\sum_{r=1}^n d_r$ positions, and each forward/back substitution solve uses $O(\sum_r d_r)$ scalar operations. These are arithmetic and factor-storage counts; they are not wall-clock or total workspace bounds.

Iterating gives side lengths at depth $r$ at most $s_r=\lceil k/2^r\rceil$. There are at most $2^{dr}$ boxes at that depth because each box has at most $2^d$ children. By depth $R=\lceil\log_2 k\rceil$, every side has length $1$, so all remaining boxes are terminal. For $0\le r\le R$, $k/2^r\ge1/2$, hence $s_r\le2k/2^r$.

If $k=1$, the grid and its ordering contain one terminal pivot and its factor column contains only the diagonal. Hence $d_v=1$ for its unique vertex, and [F3] gives $O(1)$ work and exactly one stored factor entry.

Let $G'$ be the structural graph of $A$ and let $G$ be the full nearest-neighbor grid on the same vertices. They use the same coordinate ordering. If a pair is an edge in a filled graph of $G'$, [F3] supplies a witness walk in $G'$ with internal vertices eliminated earlier; since $G'$ is a subgraph of $G$, the same walk witnesses that edge in the corresponding filled graph of $G$. Thus every later filled neighbor in $G'$ is also one in $G$, and each subgraph column size is at most the full-grid column size. Fix a box at depth $r$. Its separator has at most $d s_r^{d-1}$ vertices by the union bound over its at most $d$ median hyperplanes; the terminal singleton satisfies the same bound. By [F2], each such pivot has full-grid column size at most $3d s_r^{d-1}$, so the same bound holds for $A$.

The factorization work contributed by one depth-$r$ box is therefore at most a constant depending only on $d$ times $s_r^{d-1}s_r^{2(d-1)}=s_r^{3(d-1)}$, using [F4]. Summing over at most $2^{dr}$ boxes at each depth and using $s_r\le2k/2^r$ gives [step 2.1, F4, algebra]
$$
O\!\left(k^{3(d-1)}\sum_{r=0}^{R}2^{-r(2d-3)}\right).
$$
For $d=2$, the geometric ratio is $2^{-1}$, so this is $O(k^3)$. For $d=3$, the ratio is $2^{-3}$, so it is $O(k^6)$.

The storage contributed by one depth-$r$ box is at most a constant times $s_r^{d-1}s_r^{d-1}=s_r^{2(d-1)}$, again by [F2] and [F4]. Summing over boxes and using $s_r\le2k/2^r$ gives [step 2.1, F2, F4, algebra]
$$
O\!\left(k^{2(d-1)}\sum_{r=0}^{R}2^{-r(d-2)}\right).
$$
For $d=2$, there are $O(\log k)$ equal-order terms, giving $O(k^2\log k)$. For $d=3$, the series is bounded by $\sum_{r\ge0}2^{-r}=2$, giving $O(k^4)$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\in\mathbb N$ (including $0$), and let $A\in M_{n\times n}(F)$ satisfy
$A_{ij}=A_{ji}$ for every $i,j<n$ (that is, $A$ is symmetric). Its
**structural graph** is
the simple undirected graph $G_0=(V,E_0)$ with vertex set
$V=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and edge set

$$E_0:=\bigl\{\{i,j\}:0\le i<j<n,\ A_{ij}\ne0\bigr\}.$$

An **elimination ordering** is a listing $v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}$ in which every
vertex of $V$ occurs exactly once. Define the current vertex set by
$V_k=\{v_\ell:k\le\ell<n\}$, starting with the structural graph $G_0$. At
step $k$, the **later neighbors** of $v_k$ are

$$N_k(v_k):=\{u\in V_k\setminus\{v_k\}:\{u,v_k\}\in E_k\}.$$

The filled graph $G_{k+1}=(V_{k+1},E_{k+1})$ is obtained by deleting $v_k$ and
its incident edges, retaining all edges between remaining vertices, and adding
every edge between two distinct vertices of $N_k(v_k)$. An edge added at step
$k$ that was not already in $E_k$ is a **fill edge**. Repeating this rule
defines the symbolic elimination pattern for the ordering; it is defined from
the initial graph and ordering alone, without numerical pivot values.

If $N_k(v_k)$ is nonempty, the **parent** of $v_k$ is the later neighbor
$v_\ell$ with least position $\ell>k$ in the ordering. If $N_k(v_k)$ is
empty, $v_k$ is a root. Each non-root has a unique parent, and positions strictly increase along parent edges, so there is no directed cycle. If the underlying undirected graph had a cycle, its least-position vertex would be a child of both adjacent later vertices, contradicting uniqueness. Thus the parent relation is an elimination forest.

Write a vector as $x=(x_0,y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The quadratic form is $x^TAx=x_0^2+\sum_i y_i^2+2t x_0\sum_i y_i$. Since $m\sum_i y_i^2-(\sum_i y_i)^2=\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2\ge0$, we have $|\sum_i y_i|\le\sqrt m\,\|y\|_2$. Therefore [given, algebra]
$$2t|x_0|\left|\sum_i y_i\right|\le 2t\sqrt m\,|x_0|\|y\|_2\le t\sqrt m(x_0^2+\|y\|_2^2)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2.$$
It follows that $x^TAx\ge\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2>0$ for $x\ne0$, so $A$ is positive definite.

In leaf-first order, each leaf has exactly one later neighbor, the center. By [F1] no pair of distinct remaining neighbors exists, so eliminating that leaf adds no edge. This holds for every leaf; eliminating the last center also adds no edge.

In center-first order, the center's later-neighbor set is all $m$ leaves. By [F1], the graph update inserts every pair of distinct leaves, so it has $\binom m2$ leaf-to-leaf fill edges not in the original star.

The pivot at the center is $1$. Its Schur complement on the leaves is $I_m-t^2\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$, whose off-diagonal entries are $-t^2\ne0$. Thus the symbolic fill edges from step 1.3 are also numerical nonzeros for this matrix, while step 1.2 gives no fill in the other order.

Input an integer $k\ge1$ and dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. The coordinate vertices are $\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d$. Identify them with the zero-based matrix indices $0,\ldots,k^d-1$ by the lexicographic bijection $q(i_1,\ldots,i_d)=\sum_{a=1}^d i_a k^{d-a}$. The grid graph has an edge between two coordinate vertices exactly when they differ by $1$ in one coordinate and agree in all others. Use the graph and ordering conventions of [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]] on these indices. Thus $d=2$ gives the five-point graph and $d=3$ the seven-point graph.

Order a rectangular coordinate subbox recursively as follows. For each coordinate whose side length is at least $2$, choose its lower median coordinate, namely the coordinate with $\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor$ positions below it in a side of length $m$. Let $S$ be the union of the coordinate hyperplanes at those selected medians. Delete $S$, obtaining at most $2^d$ nonempty rectangular child boxes. Recursively order the child boxes in lexicographic order of their lower corners, then append the vertices of $S$ in lexicographic order. If no coordinate has side length at least $2$, append the remaining vertex as a terminal separator. Apply this rule first to the whole grid. The resulting order is the **coordinate nested-dissection ordering**.

The recursion uses only the graph geometry. It makes no fill or complexity claim for arbitrary graphs.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, $k\ge2$, and $n=k^d$. Identify the coordinate grid $\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d$ with the zero-based matrix indices by the lexicographic bijection in [[alg-nested-dissection-ordering-on-regular-grids]]. Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite, with structural graph a subgraph of the $d$-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid. Under the coordinate nested-dissection ordering, exact scalar multifrontal Cholesky has
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
d&\text{arithmetic work}&\text{symbolic factor storage}\\
2&O(n^{3/2})&O(n\log n)\\
3&O(n^2)&O(n^{4/3}).
\end{array}
$$
The storage is the number of allocated factor entries, including structural zeros, and excludes temporary contribution arrays. The bounds use the stated grid geometry; they assert no general-graph bound. For $k=1$, there is one pivot and both work and factor storage are $O(1)$.

For every grid vertex $v$, let $b(v)=4-\deg_{G_k}(v)$ be its number of missing boundary neighbors. Expanding squares gives [given, algebra]
$$x^TA_kx=\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E(G_k)}(x_v-x_w)^2+\sum_{v\in G_k}b(v)x_v^2.$$
The right side is nonnegative. If it is zero, every adjacent pair has equal coordinates and every boundary vertex with $b(v)>0$ has value zero. The grid is connected and has a boundary vertex, so all coordinates are equal to zero. Hence $A_k$ is positive definite.

By [F1], the order is the coordinate nested-dissection order on the five-point grid. The matrix is symmetric positive definite by step 1.1 and its off-diagonal pattern is exactly $G_k$. Any invalid operation, nonfinite output or nonzero exact intermediate outside the normal range returns `range-failure`. Hermitian counterparts, sign changes and conjugation are exact copies.

For a complex value $z=x+iy$, $|z|$ denotes its exact mathematical modulus $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$; this convention does not add a modulus operation to the floating-point model. Each field operation or comparison consumes one unit of the nonnegative integer controller budget; a fixed power is expanded into its stated finite chain of multiplications. For binary/rational stored values and rational $u,\theta$, exact rational arithmetic implements this controller with finite integers; no bit-complexity bound is claimed. Compute each of $(1-u)^4,(1+u)^4,(1+u)^5$ by left-associated repeated multiplication. These prescribed finite expression trees and finite input loops fix the guard procedure and its budget count. Scalar pivots satisfy the same scalar threshold argument.

Define $R=\widehat J/(s\widehat d)$ for analysis only. Scaling gives $\|\widehat J-J\|_F\le u\|J\|_F\le\sqrt2u\|J\|_2$. The inverse formula gives $\|D^{-1}\|_2=\|J\|_2/(s|\det E|)$, and step 1.1 gives $|\det E|/|\widehat d|\le1+\mu$. The computed $B/s$ has Frobenius error at most $u\|B\|_F/s$. By [F2], its product with $\widehat J$ adds at most $g_2(1+u)\|B\|_F\|\widehat J\|_F/s$. Since $\|\widehat J\|_F\le\sqrt2\|\widehat J\|_2$, the product discrepancy relative to $B\widehat J/s$ is at most $(\sqrt2g_2(1+u)+u)\|B\|_F\|\widehat J\|_2/s$. Put $H=\widehat M-M$. Direct block multiplication gives the displayed full residual, because $N=HD$ and $\widehat MD\widehat M^*-MB^*=HB^*+\widehat MN^*$. The Hermitian off-diagonal matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&N^*\\N&0\end{pmatrix}$ has norm $\|N\|_2$: its square is block diagonal with $N^*N,NN^*$, or equivalently use the defining singular-value maximum. Also $\|N\|_2\le e_M\|D\|_2$. Triangle inequality and step 2.2 therefore give $\|F\|_2\le f$.
